# Arguments for Rigorous AI Training Data Transparency

## What do “frontier AI labs” actually train their models on? Do we know? Do they even know? There are arguments to be made we should all know, and in detail.

--

Listen

Share

The importance of training data for LLM output can’t be overstated. And with the public internet having been crawled to the end, the large model providers exceedingly look for other data sources to add to their corpus. How much do we know about what LLMs are trained on?

Do the companies even know any more, or do they blindly trust their tool chains to sort it out? Should we know? What arguments can be made for a more rigorous transparency? Can generative AI ever be “trustworthy” without it?

This article will argue that total and fine-grained transparency about the sources of training material would greatly benefit the ability to judge models.

### Garbage in

In recent weeks, the question “What was your model trained on?” has emerged in two very different cases:

In the “Navier-Stoke affair” over OpenAI’s claim to have solved a longstanding math problem, a mathematician wondered if OpenAI accessed his material on OpenAI Codex for training purposes . When confronted, OpenAI just stated ominously that “can’t rule it out”.

Meanwhile, in a lawsuit against Elon Musk’s SpaceX AI, a plaintiff alleges that Grok was trained using pictures of her abuse to generate new illegal pornographic images (Nick Robins-Early, The Guardian 2026). More generally, the lawsuit alleges that the chatbot has derived its capability to generate non-consensual sexual material by being trained on such material because xAI has no filter on its training material in place:

> xAI’s publicly stated datafiltering practices name violent content as an example of what’s excluded from training, but do not specify CSAM, NCII, or NSFW material as excluded categories. (Case 5:26-cv-09016-NC)

Now it could be that OpenAI is just playing it safe and attempts to keep it vague for legal reasons, but it is also possible that the companies have lost the ability to monitor and review training material due to its sheer size and time pressure.

### The privacy question

At this point, the publicly accessible web has been largely sucked dry by AI crawlers, which has caused them to a) turn to offline material such as physical books and documents and b) turn their attention to non-public data such as chats or cloud storage.

All large model providers train their models on their clients chatbot conversations by default (at least outside the EU), a feature that users can turn off in their privacy settings, but unlikely to do so. In fact, a survey found that 53% of users are not aware that their chatbot conversations become training material (Valdes 2026).

The motivation behind this “default” setting is obvious, as I can’t think of no reason why someone would deliberately enable this feature without gaining any advantage from it.

It is interesting that all large model providers make exceptions for their business plans: If their tools are so reliable in filtering out personal data, why is there a concern for business? The answer is simply that enterprise customers will have the legal firepower when information leaks, something the average user lacks.

### What we want to know, and why?

Model providers should be mandated to provide a complete list of documents used for training (source, type, access time). In addition, companies should be mandated to lay out what percentage of their training data falls into certain categories, such as: Public information, offline information, private information (such as chatbot session, cloud storage etc), and this information should be public to at least a certain extent.

The benefits are plenty:

- It would tell us a lot more about data governance at the large model providers, and the transparency would in turn put pressure on the providers.

- It would tell us to what extent privacy is respected, and allow for a detailed assessment if data is appropriately cleaned.

- It would give outside researchers a change to review the training material for obvious sources of bias, and disclose if model providers deliberately or accidentally train on biased input, poisoned or manipulated data sets.

- It would help to assess to what extent models are trained on other models output.

- It would help legal discovery in cases of privacy and copyright

- Analysing the extent to which “semantic interference” occurs , without relying on a later explanation from the provider.

- Identifying what weight (by percentage) is given to sources, what impact they have on the overall corpus.

This is not a conclusive list.

Before we deal with the arguments the AI industry will bring up against this, let’s look at current regulations that have (or plan to have) some form of transparency requirements when it comes to training data.

### Current regulatory requirements are falling short

The EU AI Act mandates GPAI providers in Article 53.1(d) to “ draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary about the content used for training of the general-purpose AI model, according to a template provided by the AI Office. ”

The template mentioned has recently been specified in the “ Explanatory Notice and Template for the Public Summary of Training Content ”. It specifies the data as “ all sources and types of data, regardless of whether the data are protected or not, including by an intellectual property right. ” (EU Explanatory Notice 2026 )

> [..] this section requires disclosure of the main datasets that were used to train the model, such as large private or public databases, and a comprehensive narrative description of the data scraped online by or on behalf of the provider (including a summary of the most relevant domain names scraped) and a narrative description of all other data sources used (e.g. user data or synthetic data) to ensure completeness of the summary regarding the content used for the model training (EU Explanatory Notice )

While those requirements are extensive, they may not be detailed enough for the purposes we outlined. More importantly, there appears to be no mechanism for anyone outside the regulator to access this information.

> The lack of access to a complete list of datasets diminishes the ability of parties with legitimate interests to exercise their rights under EU law, including the protection of copyright and personal data. As a result, this approach would lead to reduced transparency and accountability of GPAI model providers. (Warso 2025)

Furthermore, without an audit of the submitted reports and no information on the impact a source had on the training corpus, the information provides only some but limited insight.

> There is no audit. Every flag is self-asserted; nothing external confirms that a “no” on crawled data or user data is accurate. And the template asks whether a source was used, never how much. (Maynard 2026)

Meanwhile, just last month, the Japanese government approved the draft of the “AI Panel’s” rules on disclosing training data. Again though, the focus appears to be on copyright violation, not on data quality or privacy.

More concerningly, the Japanese government appears to favour a “comply or explain” approach, and make the rules a nonbinding code, “allowing them to choose either to comply with the code or publicly explain why they will not comply” (The Japan Times 2026).

It is to be feared that such a quasi-voluntary approach will do little in an industry driven by time and efficiency pressure.

### The industry has, and will continue, to push back

So, how much should regulators or independent researchers be allowed to know? The AI industry that has already lobbied against self-assessed reports in the past would surely drag out the same defences against a detailed and public reporting requirement.

- It will argue that the burden of transparency will “stifle innovation”, however accuracy in training data governance can hardly be called anti innovation.

- It will claim that training data sources are a trade secret. That, too, is a questionable argument. While the vast amount of public information has already been accessed by everyone else, the non-public data sources can’t be accessed even if the sources are disclosed. It would therefore not be of much benefit to competitors.

### Conclusion

Of course AI regulation should not stop there, but improving on training data transparency would go a long way in accountability.

The EU AI Act moves into the right direction, but the lack of publicly available data and lack of audit is worrying. A system that only looks at the submitted data in case of incidents will do little in an industry that is hungry for data and considers privacy as a probability vector only.

If the black box is to be made transparent, we need to start at the source.

# With a Shovel of Salt: AI Success Stories and the Retraction Gap

## AI success stories regularly appear in the media. Their retractions later receive comparably little attention, while their impact persists.

--

Listen

Share

Ever since generative AI has become all the rage, the media has been flooded with success stories: Breakthroughs in science, improved results in education, a more efficient health system, increased productivity in enterprise.

Some of these stories have later been retracted. But there is a multidimensional gap between the reported success and retraction: A gap in time, a discrepancy in attention and the influence both have over decisions: the “retraction gap”.

### Introduction

For the industry, there is a lot at stake. As is for many governments, not only because of financial but also political entanglement: Many have firmly tied their hope for economic growth to the success of AI, even justifying their reluctance to regulate.

The narrative of inevitability of AI in all aspects of society, as “revolutionary” new industrial revolution, demands success stories especially in areas that are perceived to need “new solutions”. Some of those success stories have later been questions, or outright found to be misleading or false. The reporting of those successes is not necessarily deliberate deception, but part of the natural media cycle.

What is important is the gap between reported success and retraction, which can measure years, and the discrepancy between the amount of publicity the success story has received vs the retraction can be significant. Often ignored is the fact that decisions have already been made based on alleged success that will not get reversed even if the underlying story is discredited.

While not unique to the AI industry, this phenomenon is more pronounced here because of the immense “fear of missing out” pressure.

First we should look at five examples selected from very diverse fields where the overly optimistic assessments of AI have been retracted, and why neither academia nor politics is immune from the issue.

### 1. ChatGPT the education booster

One of the most prominent studies that has been recently retracted by a major scientific journal was a study that assessed “ the effectiveness of ChatGPT in improving students’ learning performance ”. Originally published in May 2025, it was retracted by Nature a year later.

With 549,000 accesses and 420 citations the paper received considerable attention, likely because it appeared to offer a solution in a field where people were especially concerned about the impact of AI.

The paper was interestingly specific in its assessment, solely focusing on ChatGPT as a tool in education:

“ In summary, the meta-analysis results of this study confirm the positive impacts of ChatGPT on learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking […] ChatGPT could be actively incorporated into STEM and related courses ” (Wang, Fan 2025). The paper ends in a glowing endorsement and recommendations:

“(2) the broad use of ChatGPT at various grade levels and in different types of courses should be encouraged to support diverse learning needs; […] 5) ChatGPT should be flexibly integrated into teaching as an intelligent tutor, learning partner, and educational tool.” ( Wang, Fan 2025 )

The lack of critical distance should likely have raised eyebrows, especially because evaluating a chatbot represent a specific snapshot in time.

The journal decided to retract this article, in its own words, due to concerns relating to “d iscrepancies in the meta‑analysis ”, sadly without giving specific details. “Taken together, the identified issues undermine the Editor’s confidence in the validity of the analysis and the conclusions drawn from it.” (Nature 2026)

The distance between publication, ravish reviews and retraction was about a year, but a significant year when it comes to adoption of AI in education.

Meanwhile, a large study by the OECD recently came to a very different conclusion: AI can be useful in education, but only if it is used in a way that challenges the student: “At first glance, the PISA data aren’t positive: Students who are using AI chatbots for specific tasks such as summarising texts get lower scores in science, on average, than those who don’t.” and concludes that there is little exceptional about AI: “ Where technology enables or enhances that cognitive struggle, students will advance. Where technology short-circuits the productive struggle of learning, it will undercut students’ development.” (OECD 2026)

### 2. The perfect paper at the perfect time

A paper published at MIT in 2024 bundled two interesting claims together: That “ AI-assisted scientist discovered 44% more materials ” while AI is causing job dissatisfaction for those scientists. We covered this paper and its retraction in details in the article “ The Curious Case Of That Withdrawn MIT AI Paper ” in 2025.

> For journalists it was also about breaching the gap of praising our brilliant new AI future and concerns of their readers, spurred by expectations of a “white collar job wipe out”. The paper fit this narrative perfectly, at the right time. (Misaliged 2025)

The retraction notice was curiously reported in the Wall Street Journal, and for good reason: The Journal had prominently featured the paper, and most prominently the author in December 2024.

### 3. “AI-generated figure containing nonsense”

When asked about the potential benefits of generative AI, medical science is often cited as a prime example: The promise that AI will literally “ cure cancer ” is as much as a meme as it is a frequent argument by AI influencers.

Medical studies often take years to conduct, and more time to be verified independently. The study “ Bridging the gap: explainable AI for autism diagnosis and parental support with TabPFNMix and SHAP ”, published in Nature in 2025 appeared to report on promising results:

“The findings of this research reinforced the reliability of the proposed framework and its potential applicability in clinical settings, offering clinicians and caregivers a transparent and accurate AI-assisted diagnostic tool.” (Jiang 2025)

For once, not only did the retraction come only two months after publication, it also did not hold back:

“ Post-publication investigation confirmed that the paper does not contain an adequate description of the framework it proposes, uses an AI-generated figure containing nonsense to demonstrate the framework, and does not include code underlying the model developed. ” (Nature 2026)

The retraction here shines a light on the complexity of peer review in the age of AI. Even under traditional circumstances research data is hard to judge from the outside, but even more so if it involves claims related to generative AI.

### 4. The consultants: Hallucinated adoption

Whenever a new technology arrives that targets enterprise and governments, the consultant companies play an essential role in its adoption.

In 2026, it emerged that a KPMG report on how AI is being used by businesses across the world was found to have exaggerated the adoption of the technology with bogus case studies that ironically appear to have been based on AI hallucinations. The report was found to have made numerous false claims, including about the adoption of AI at UBS, the UK’s National Health Service, Swiss Federal Railways and Transport for London (Bratton, Foley 2026).

Another report, published by EY (formerly known as Earnest & Young), had claimed in October 2025 that its AI-related revenue had grown 30 per cent in the previous year and 15,000 staff had worked on client projects “ranging from delivering enterprise-wide transformations to AI governance frameworks that help drive the responsible implementation of AI” (Foley 2026). The report turned out to have contained “ included apparent AI hallucinations and fake footnotes ”.

As researchers from GPTZero point out: “ When the report includes fake information […] it can ‘poison the well’ by misleading future researchers, especially if the report is published by a well-known consulting firm and hosted on a high-traffic website. ” (Foley 2026)

The sway consultant companies have over governments and enterprise can hardly be overstated. The studies will have been cited at business conferences and undoubtedly made their way into internal business presentation.

Consultants play another important role: They help companies to “outsource trust”: If it is a success, the credit will go to company management. If it goes wrong, or emerges to be based on false data, the blame can at least be put on the consultants. A mechanism that does not inspire a critical approach to consultant studies.

### 5. NHS England and Palantir: Correlation vs causation

The involvement of American company Palantir in the British health system has been controversial from the start, with concerns ranging from international politics, the ideology of the company’s founders to data privacy concerns.

NHS England originally suggested that Palantir’s federated data platform has contributed to 110,000 additional operations being carried out. Those figures were widely cited in the media and left little doubt about the causation: Palantir allegedly helps to reduce the NHS waiting list.

Anyone familiar with the discourse around the NHS will know that the issue of waiting lists is a hotly debated one, often presented as the crucial data point to judge the effectiveness of the British health system. Extremely emotionally charged, it and has been a focus of the political fight between government and opposition for more than a decade.

> Government ministers — and Palantir — have long promoted benefits from the Federated Data Platform (FDP), software provided by the US tech giant. A page on NHS England’s website titled: ‘NHS Federated Data Platform uptake and benefits’ includes a number of claims, such as “111,589 — Total number of additional patients undergoing procedures in theatres”. (Foxglove 2026)

It has recently been suggested that the software’s effectiveness is questionable, something the NHS has somewhat quietly admitted:

> “This is an observational before/after comparison showing changes to this metric following the introduction of the NHS FDP Inpatient theatre module. We cannot therefore draw conclusions about cause and effect as other variables have not been controlled for.” (Foxglove 2026)

In fact, it looks like a classical case of mixing up causation and correlation:

> “A number of improvements in NHS performance attributed to Palantir have been driven by just a handful of hospitals, according to data that shows some trusts have actually delivered fewer operations since adopting the technology.” […] “Where trusts have reported significant improvements, it is not clear how much this reflects FDP adoption as the figures are not adjusted for other factors, such as trusts investing in more staff or weekend clinics.” (Financial Times 2025)

The NHS/Palantir example shows how the burden of proof has been shifted to the critics once a system has been introduced, even if questions emerge and claims are “quietly” retracted.
